source_note: Original concise formulations grounded in Hansen and Quinn, Unit 1, Sections 13-17, printed pages 17-30.

grammar_rules.title: Greek nouns mark gender, number, and case

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: Every Greek noun has grammatical gender, number, and case; these categories must be identified separately.

examples.note: Masculine, singular, nominative in the cited form.

exceptions: The dual exists in Greek but is relatively rare and is not developed in Unit 1.

grammar_rules.title: Inflection consists of stem and ending

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: A declined noun consists of a stem carrying the lexical meaning and an ending marking grammatical information such as case and number.

examples.note: Stem λόγ- plus nominative singular ending -ος.

grammar_rules.title: Nominative case functions

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: The nominative commonly marks the subject, a predicate nominative, or the name of a thing.

grammar_rules.title: Genitive case functions

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: The genitive may express dependence or limitation, often translated with of, and may also express separation or motion away from.
exceptions: English of does not always correspond to a Greek genitive.

grammar_rules.title: Dative case functions

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: The dative may mark an interested party, instrument or accompaniment, and location in place or time.
exceptions: English to indicating motion toward is not equivalent to the Greek dative.

grammar_rules.title: Accusative case functions

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: The accusative commonly marks the direct object and may express motion toward or extent in space or time.

grammar_rules.title: Vocative case function

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: The vocative marks a noun being addressed directly.

grammar_rules.title: Derive a noun stem from the genitive singular

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: To decline a noun, take the genitive singular, remove its genitive ending, and attach the endings of the noun's declension to the resulting stem.

grammar_rules.title: First-declension feminine patterns

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: Unit 1 first-declension feminine nouns use the singular patterns in -η or -ᾱ and share the same plural endings.
exceptions: The distribution of -η and -ᾱ in the singular depends on the stem environment described in Section 14.

grammar_rules.title: First-declension genitive plural accent

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: The genitive plural of first-declension nouns ends in -ῶν with a circumflex on the ultima.

grammar_rules.title: Persistent noun accent

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: A noun's accent normally remains on the same syllable and of the same type as far as the general accent rules permit.

examples.note: The accent remains on the penult.

exceptions: Required accent changes include the first-declension genitive plural and changes forced by vowel quantity.

grammar_rules.title: Final -αι and -οι count short for accent

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: For the accentuation rules taught here, final -αι and -οι count as short vowels.

grammar_rules.title: Second-declension masculine and feminine pattern

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: Second-declension masculine and feminine nouns generally have nominative singular -ος and share the same case endings.
exceptions: Gender must be learned from the vocabulary entry; an -ος noun is not necessarily masculine.

grammar_rules.title: Neuter nominative, accusative, and vocative identity

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: In every neuter noun, the nominative, accusative, and vocative are identical within each number.

grammar_rules.title: Neuter plural ending

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: The nominative, accusative, and vocative plural ending of neuter nouns is -α.

grammar_rules.title: Article agrees with its noun

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: The Greek article agrees with the noun it modifies in gender, number, and case, whether or not their endings look alike.

grammar_rules.title: Attributive position

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: A word group that limits a noun is in attributive position when an agreeing article places it with that noun; Unit 1 introduces article-modifier-noun, repeated-article, and postposed-article patterns.

examples.translation: the words, namely those of the brother

exceptions: A possessive genitive commonly appears in attributive position but may also stand outside it.

grammar_rules.title: Principal uses of the article in Unit 1

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: The article may identify particular persons or things, denote a generic class, accompany abstract nouns and familiar names, or supply a possessive sense when context makes the possessor clear.
exceptions: The article may be omitted with something unique and well known when the context is clear.

grammar_rules.title: Inflection permits flexible word order

source.work: Hansen and Quinn, Greek: An Intensive Course

grammar_rules.statement: Because endings identify grammatical relations, Greek word order can vary to express emphasis, contrast, balance, or variety rather than merely identifying subject and object.

examples.translation: It is his brother Homer educates.

exceptions: Interpretive emphasis depends on context; word order alone should not be treated mechanically.
